source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with LLMs
finding: A separate repair model, given the failed proof and the Isabelle error message, fixes proofs the generator got wrong.
numbers: PISA test set, 6,336 theorems. Generate once (temp 0) then repair once: +266 theorems (+4.2%). Generate alone at 16 samples 34.8%, at 64 samples 40.7%.
limits: Fine-tuned Minerva 8b/62b. Possible test leakage via pretraining (authors flag it).
agent_relevance: S5 REVISE: feed the checker's exact error text back with the failed attempt.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with LLMs
finding: Cost-matched, repair beats resampling, but only when it sees the error message. A repair model without the error message did not beat plain generation at equal inference cost.
numbers: Figure 5: Generate+Repair above Generate for the same number of attempts; Generate+Repair (no err msg) does not surpass Generate.
limits: Read from a plot; no exact per-point numbers extracted. One repair per distinct failed proof.
agent_relevance: The gain comes from the error signal, not from a second try. Revision without new information is just resampling.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with LLMs
finding: Repeated repair has diminishing returns: a second repair adds little and only modestly beats pure resampling at the same cost.
numbers: Inference cost 2: 24.9%. Second repair (cost 3): 26.2% (+1.3). Plain generation at cost 3: 25.4%. Repair wins by 0.8 points.
limits: Greedy temp 0. Authors say repair training data covers only first-error cases, so later rounds are out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Cap revision rounds low; later rounds need training or prompts that match the error type.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with LLMs
finding: Adding theory-file context (nearby proofs) helps more than model size or repair.
numbers: 8b generate at 64 samples: 40.7% to 47.5% with context. 62b with context: 47.9% (only +0.4 over 8b at 64 samples; +1.3 at 16 samples).
limits: Context helps by letting the model copy and adapt nearby proofs.
agent_relevance: REVISE should retrieve similar solved items; Rango measures the same lever.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with LLMs
finding: Repair and a symbolic search tool are complementary.
numbers: Baldur 8b with context plus Thor union: 65.7%, vs Thor alone 58.0% and Baldur alone 47.9%. Sledgehammer 25.6%, search-based LM approach 39.0%.
limits: Union of two systems, not a single pipeline.
agent_relevance: Mix a symbolic checker/solver with the LLM reviser rather than relying on one.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Study of LLM-written Coq proof errors: most are fixable by rules. Wrong theorem application 49.6%, invalid reference 15.2%, incorrect rewrite 11.7%, redundant intros 10.8%, tactic misuse 8.5%, bullet misuse 3.7%, other 0.6%.
numbers: Formative study on Verdi theorems, GPT-3.5 proofs.
limits: One project and one model family for the taxonomy.
agent_relevance: Typed error classes allow targeted repair operators instead of generic 'try again'.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Generate-then-repair with symbolic repair plus backtracking beats strong baselines on CoqGym.
numbers: 10,842 theorems: PALM(GPT-3.5) 4,377 (40.4%). Passport 14.4%, Proverbot9001 17.1%, DSP 22.9%. GPT-3.5 alone 3.7%. PALM proves 1,270 theorems no other tool does.
limits: Large time overhead per proof; CoqGym leakage not controlled here (Cobblestone later controls it).
agent_relevance: Wrapping a weak one-shot generator in repair and backtracking gave about 11x over the bare model.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Ablation: backtracking matters far more than any single repair rule.
numbers: Without backtracking 702 (6.5%) vs 4,377 (40.4%), about 5x less in their wording. Removing one repair mechanism: 39.2%, 38.5%, 39.0%, 37.8%. Removing premise retrieval: 38.2%.
limits: Single run, single sample per theorem.
agent_relevance: Revision needs a fallback to an earlier state (S5 back to an earlier step), not only local patching.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Works across LLMs; stronger models help but repair lifts every one.
numbers: Alone: GPT-3.5 3.7%, GPT-4o 6.4%, Llama-3-70B 3.6%, Llama-3-8B 0.1%. With PALM: 40.4%, 42.6%, 38.3%, 31.7%. Union of four LLMs 5,210.
limits: Scaffold gain much larger than model-size gain.
agent_relevance: The scaffold carries most of the benefit for weak solvers.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Proof Automation with Large Language Models (PALM)
finding: Failure analysis on 100 unproven theorems: missing premises dominate.
numbers: Premises not retrieved 58, retrieved but unused 14, tactics not used 39 (categories overlap).
limits: 100-sample manual review.
agent_relevance: Repair cannot fix missing knowledge; a REVISE step should also ask what is missing.

source: Lyra: Orchestrating Dual Correction in Automated Theorem Proving (2023)
finding: Tool Correction replaces a failing proof tactic with a stronger tool (e.g. Sledgehammer) when the claim is right but the tool was too weak. Conjecture Correction regenerates a sketch using the prover's error messages.
numbers: miniF2F-test 51.2% (valid 55.3%) at 200 attempts with human informal proofs; prior SOTA 45.5% (+5.7 points). DSP at 200 attempts: 42.6% test, 50.4% valid.
limits: Table 2 layout garbled in text extraction; only prose-stated numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Distinguish 'claim wrong' from 'method too weak': two different revisions.

source: Lyra: Orchestrating Dual Correction in Automated Theorem Proving (2023)
finding: Conjecture Correction alone adds little; it needs a strong prover under it, and it needs more attempts.
numbers: miniF2F-test, human informal proofs: CC adds 0.4 points without Tool Correction and 5.3 with it. Attempts 100 to 200: DSP 39.7% to 42.6%; Lyra 47.1% to 51.2%.
limits: Authors' own reading; 200 attempts split into 40 patches of 5.
agent_relevance: Revision pays off only if the checker beneath it can close the gaps.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: Plan then fill: LLM drafts an informal proof, maps it to a formal sketch with gaps, an automated prover fills the gaps. A proof-plan-like structure with no repair.
numbers: miniF2F: 20.9% to 39.3% with sketches (38.9% with LLM-written informal proofs).
limits: Abstract and intro only. No repair loop; any gap failure kills the sketch.
agent_relevance: Plans as skeletons with checkable gaps is the learned analogue of proof planning.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: Verifier-Guided Self-Correction
finding: Adding Lean-compiler feedback self-correction (2 rounds) gives a steady gain across budgets.
numbers: MiniF2F pass@32: 32B 88.1% to 90.4%; about +2 points for both 8B and 32B. PutnamBench: +14 solves at pass@32 (57 with correction). 8B: 84.6%.
limits: Self-reported; model trained with a 50/50 generation/correction RL mix, so correction is trained, not just prompted.
agent_relevance: Correction ability may need training; plain prompting may not match this.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: Verifier-Guided Self-Correction
finding: Ablation: removing compiler error messages hurts clearly; removing earlier chain of thought hurts slightly.
numbers: With 128k context and 5 revision rounds, pass@32 averaged 92.7%, above the 92.2% of the non-correcting model at pass@8192.
limits: Figure-based; exact ablation values not extracted. Longer context needed for 5 rounds.
agent_relevance: Keep the reasoning trace of the failed attempt visible in the revision prompt; error text is the key ingredient.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover-V2: Verifier-Guided Self-Correction
finding: Correction benefits more from RL than plain generation does.
numbers: Vanilla pass@N plateaus at high RL steps; correction pass@N keeps rising. Authors cite shortage of SFT correction data.
limits: Plot-based.
agent_relevance: Revision skill is under-trained in base models; expect weak prompted revision.

source: Ospanov et al. (2025) APOLLO: Automated LLM and Lean Collaboration
finding: Repair loop: fix syntax, isolate failing sub-lemmas with Lean, try automatic solvers, call the LLM on remaining goals only, recombine, re-verify up to depth r.
numbers: Goedel-Prover-SFT miniF2F 64.7% at 25,600 samples to 65.6% with about 362 samples on average. Kimina-Prover-Distill-7B +4.2%. Goedel-V2-8B +0.9% at matched budget. o3-mini 3.3% to 40.2%; o4-mini 7.0% to 46.7% (as read from the table).
limits: Some table cells garbled; numbers from abstract and text.
agent_relevance: Localized repair (fix only the failing sub-goal) is far cheaper than whole-proof resampling.

source: Ospanov et al. (2025) APOLLO: Automated LLM and Lean Collaboration
finding: Recursion depth gives monotone gains with diminishing size.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B: 57.6% at r=0, 60.7% r=2, 63.5% r=4, 65.6% r=6 (tokens 16.1K to 179K). Second model: 63.1% base to 75.0% at r=6.
limits: Two models shown; budgets vary.
agent_relevance: Plan a fixed revision depth of about 2 to 4, not unbounded.

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover
finding: Lemma-style proof with refinement from Lean feedback, proved lemmas and self-summary beats pure pass@k.
numbers: Light setting: 8 to 16 refinements per attempt, equal to Pass@64x256. IMO 2022 P2 proved with refinement; without it only at Pass@8192. Claims 78.1% of formalized past IMO problems, over 50% PutnamBench, MiniF2F saturated.
limits: Closed model, vendor report; test-time compute not fully stated. Heavier settings use far more.
agent_relevance: Decomposing into named lemmas makes it clear which part failed, so revision is local.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback or oracle labels, LLM self-correction lowers accuracy on reasoning tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8% to 38.1% after round 1. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5% to 91.5% (round 1) and 89.0% (round 2). With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9% to 95.5%.
limits: General reasoning, not formal proof. The oracle result shows what a perfect stop signal would give.
agent_relevance: Proof repair works because the checker supplies the oracle. Revise without a real check is risky.
quote: improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available

source: Kasibatla et al. (2026) Cobblestone
finding: Divide and conquer: keep the parts of a failed proof that check, replace the failing parts, iterate. Controls for training-data leakage.
numbers: 48% of CoqGym100 and 38% of Wigderson100; about $1.25 and 14.7 minutes per run. With oracle structure or lemmas up to 58%. Beats a LinearRegen baseline (regenerate after first failure) by up to 104.8% added value.
limits: Different subsets than PALM so no direct comparison. Uses CoqHammer heavily.
agent_relevance: Partial credit: preserve verified sub-steps during revision.

source: Kasibatla et al. (2026) Cobblestone
finding: Tools are complementary and the symbolic hammer is a major share of the gain.
numbers: Rango + Cobblestone union 54% on BB5100 and 47% on PnVRocqLib100. CoqHammer contribution shown as large added value (Figure 9).
limits: Exact hammer ablation numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Pair revision with a strong symbolic closer.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving
finding: Retrieving earlier proofs from the same project at each step helps a lot.
numbers: CoqStoq, 2,226 projects: Rango 32.0% of theorems, 29% more than Tactician. Adding relevant proofs to context gives a 47% increase.
limits: Abstract and intro read; ablation tables not opened. Step-level, not repair.
agent_relevance: Revision should look up similar prior solutions.

source: Ringer et al. (2021) Proof repair across type equivalences (Pumpkin Pi)
finding: Symbolic repair: transport proofs across an equivalence between old and new types (list to vector, swapped constructors) and return tactic scripts.
numbers: Eight case studies. Constructor swap: repaired after picking from suggestions, no time saved because original tactics still worked. Adding constructors: no time saved vs the user-study engineer; repaired terms inefficient. Small factor-out: minutes saved. List to vector: hours instead of days after massaging.
limits: Case studies, not a controlled trial. Industrial user (Galois) reported an initial learning cost before returns.
agent_relevance: Repair is easy when the change is a clean equivalence and hard when meaning changes. Same boundary for revising plans.

source: Ringer et al. Replica user study of proof engineers (cited in Pumpkin Pi)
finding: Not opened. The Pumpkin Pi paper cites a user study of proof engineers whose benchmark changes (such as swapped constructors) served as repair tests.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Known only via the Pumpkin Pi paper.
agent_relevance: Shows the repair task came from real engineer change patterns.
